analysis.investment_thesis: Technichem Organics fails both legs of the Magic Formula — earnings yield is ~3.2% (P/E 31.1) and ROE is a dismal 0.12%, implying ROIC well below any acceptable threshold. There is no version of "cheap and good" that fits this stock; it is expensive and unprofitable.
key_strengths: High promoter holding (71.77%) signals skin in the game
Operates in specialty chemicals — a structurally attractive Indian export sector
Small base (96.7 Cr m-cap) leaves theoretical room for re-rating if earnings recover
key_risks: ROE of 0.12% — capital is essentially earning nothing
Earnings yield ~3.2% vs 10Y G-Sec ~7% — negative risk premium
Negligible institutional ownership (FII 1.09%, DII 1.24%) — no smart-money validation
red_flags: ROE 0.12% suggests near-zero or negative ROIC — Magic Formula disqualifier
P/E of 31x on barely-profitable earnings = extremely overvalued on EBIT/EV basis
Specialty chemicals cycle has been in downturn — margins likely compressed further
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Magic Formula perspective, this is a textbook AVOID. Earnings Yield proxy (1/PE) is ~3.2%, well below my 12% attractive threshold and even below the risk-free rate in India. Return on Capital, proxied by ROE of 0.12%, is essentially zero — the business is barely earning its keep, let alone the 20%+ ROIC I require. Ranking this against the BSE universe on both factors simultaneously would place it deep in the bottom decile; a stock must be cheap AND good, and Technichem is neither.

The qualitative story (specialty chemicals, 1996 vintage, 71.77% promoter holding) is irrelevant to the systematic framework. Even if one believed in a turnaround, paying 31x earnings for a sub-1% ROE business means you're underwriting both an earnings recovery AND multiple compression risk. The Magic Formula exists precisely to filter out such situations — let the screen do its job and skip.
